name: Zoe Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play flute in two paid community ensembles, record slow practice lines and help a senior teacher with beginner lessons. I worked at a library desk until six years ago and finished secondary school, so I am still a junior player and check fingerings with the teacher.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the work fit this stage of life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have grown children and a small mortgage. We have nine months of expenses saved and I earn well across several booked ensembles, but I have not checked what retirement income might be due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the ensemble managers that a quicker schedule is useful if it still states who gets paid. A computer cannot listen for a beginner running out of breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have paid dates for the term, nine months saved and other ensembles nearby. A cancelled night would be irritating, but it would not put the mortgage at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season I would keep the flute calls, recorded practice lines and supervised beginner pupils. I would request written paid dates for the next term, including a cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. The current work pays, and I am not being pushed into a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI practice coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and I want the senior teacher to hear a pupil before changing a fingering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you do about retirement paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a written benefits estimate this winter while keeping the paid dates. I will not treat a birthday as a cheque.

I would defend **listening to beginners** in person.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** covers one cancelled ensemble night without putting the household mortgage payment at risk.
Several **nearby ensembles** and current paid calls give options.
do: Keep **paid flute calls**, practice lines and supervised pupils this season.
Request **written paid dates** and cancellation terms for next term.
Request a **written benefits estimate** this winter while keeping paid work.
feel: I feel **calm** about current paid work and bills.
S0.quote: I will not treat a birthday as a cheque.
fieldNote: Her **nine-month reserve** and several nearby ensembles make a lost night manageable.
She has **never used AI** and asks for a benefits statement without assuming retirement income.

Request written benefits estimate this winter while keeping paid calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the musicians’ association that software may make cheap practice lines, but the tutor still needs paid time with a child. I would ask the association to protect preparation hours in the next centre contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording lines are about a quarter of my pay, and the schools may buy fewer of them. The nine-month reserve helps me search, but I would notice that fee loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would take the practice invoices to the association and ask the school for written paid teaching and preparation hours. In the first year, if recording fees fall, I would keep ensemble calls and apply for a posted paid school music aide role only if my secondary schooling and supervised experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and the bus timetable works; I would not leave until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing the recording fees. I have time to look, but I cannot pretend my junior lessons replace the lost sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new AI part writer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after paid training, school approval for local storage and a test on my own nameless part that the senior teacher checks by ear. I would stop if it changes a note or sends the file away, but I am not committing to use it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a verbal school opening be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would answer a real posted paid vacancy with written hours, not a friendly hint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the ensembles that AGI by 2028 can make practice lines quickly. I would ask managers to sign the paid playing and teaching dates before we set a term calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the recording fees to end in 2028 and some schools may reduce assistant hours. Robots able to play flute come around 2031, three years later. I could lose a quarter of my pay before a robot holds a flute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total practice invoices and request signed paid ensemble dates. In the first year after 2028, if paid assistant hours fall too, I would apply for a posted adult-music aide job only if my secondary schooling and supervised teaching qualify, written net pay after travel covers the lost work and the bus fits; I would keep flute calls and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the expected recording loss, but nine months saved and several local openings give me some control. A second cut to paid teaching would hurt more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a teaching certificate now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real posted aide job requires it and the course has funded tuition or paid study hours. I would not buy an unneeded certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60 if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 60 in 2028, but I have not seen a written retirement estimate. I would request one and keep working until the figures are real.

Apply for **posted adult-music aide** after 2028 assistant cuts if qualified; written net after travel covers losses, bus fits.
Keep **flute calls/pupils** until signed offer; request retirement estimate; take required teaching course only for posted job with funded tuition/paid study.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost fees but able to search locally.
S2.quote: I could lose a quarter of my pay before a robot holds a flute.
fieldNote: Her **2028 recording loss** precedes flute-playing robots around 2031.
The **aide move** needs actual assistant cuts, a qualified posted job, written net replacement, bus access and signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the school that five years until AGI by 2031 gives us time to see whether adults will pay for a live flute circle. The supervising teacher must have a wage, not just a thank-you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice-line sales may end by 2031, and playing robots could come around 2034. A paid circle might replace some fees if the adults book before we hire a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would offer a six-week beginner flute circle only if the senior teacher agrees to supervise, the centre commits a room and hire price in writing, and eight adults prepay enough for rent, inspected loan flutes, her wage and my teaching and preparation. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat only while eight paid places still cover both wages including my preparation, room and safe instruments; otherwise I would keep my paid ensemble and pupil hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing practice-line income, even while testing a paid circle without risking our reserve. I would still refund rather than ask the teacher to work free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a loan flute is unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre technician must inspect each flute before it reaches a learner. The adult can bring a safe instrument; if that place cancels and fewer than eight people pay, I would replace the booking or defer and refund everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only four adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund them and keep the paid ensemble dates. Four fees will not cover two teachers and the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the association that ten years until AGI by 2036 gives us time to demand written paid preparation. I would not tell younger players to plan retirement from a birthday alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording work may end by 2036 and flute-playing robots could reach ensembles around 2039. We have nine months saved and several local options now, but I still want a written view of retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this term I would request a written benefits estimate, ask the association for a paid two-year preparation agreement and save ten percent of each extra paid ensemble fee after mortgage, food and bus fares, aiming for twelve months while protecting six. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid flute calls and pupils and, if music fees fall, apply for a posted senior-centre music aide job only if my schooling qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost recording and playing fees and bus service works; I would leave only on a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the far end, not unsafe about next month’s bills. Knowing the actual benefits estimate would help me decide how long to keep playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra ensemble fee arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save nothing new that week. The six-month floor stays untouched instead of becoming a training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036, but I have set no retirement date. I would decide after seeing the estimate and the paid work still offered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the practice recordings could disappear before I know what teaching hours the school will still pay. Signed school hours, a real posted aide job and bus access would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the supervising teacher when a class is cancelled. A junior player cannot replace a trained teacher with a free promise.

headlineQuote: A junior player cannot replace a trained teacher with a free promise.
portrait: At **58**, Zoe is a junior flutist who moved from library work and completed secondary school.
Her higher **musician pay**, nine-month reserve and several local ensembles support current security despite junior skill.
She has **never used AI** and would seek paid instruction and school privacy approval before any trial.
A **paid flute circle** needs senior supervision, eight prepayments, written room hire, safe instruments and both wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove recording fees before she knows if assistant hours remain paid.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed paid hours**, a qualified posted aide role with written net pay and workable bus service would help Zoe.
